title: Ethos commission math: what agents take
subtitle: Working backward from the S-1 and the 80% agent tier
body:
In my post on why I'm selling Ethos, I said agents get most of each agent sale. Ethos stopped disclosing that split after its IPO, so this post walks through what Ethos pays agents, what agents are selling, and how I estimated the split for Q3.

Two percentages make this confusing. Agents are paid a percentage of the customer's premium. Their share of Ethos's revenue is a percentage of what Ethos books, which is a different number.

How Ethos gets paid

Ethos doesn't collect premiums. The customer pays the insurance carrier, and the carrier pays Ethos a commission. Life insurance commissions are quoted as a percentage of the policy's first-year premium, and almost all of it comes in the first year. Renewals are small, a few percent a year, and many term products pay none.

Ethos books the full expected lifetime commission as revenue the day a policy activates. That amount is net of expected cancellations. Carriers claw back commission when a policy lapses early, and renewals only come in on policies that stay in force.

Agent pay works the same way. Ethos books it upfront, net of the clawbacks it expects to collect from agents on early lapses. That's where Q1's one-time $16.5M charge came from. Policies lapsed less than Ethos expected, so it clawed back less agent pay and had to book more.

What Ethos pays agents

Ethos's agent terms pay producers a fee on the first 12 months of premium. Here is the compensation table from those terms, as a % of first-year premium:

TierIn-force premium neededEthos Term PrimeEthos Term ChoiceTruStage TermTruStage Advantage Whole LifeTruStage Guaranteed Acceptance Whole Life
100%$10,000100%81%61%66%36%
95%$2,50095%79.5%59.5%64.5%34.5%
90%$55090%78%58%63%33%
85%$25085%76.5%56.5%61.5%31.5%
80%$080%75%55%60%30%

In-force premium is annualized. The table also says large agencies can discuss additional options with Ethos.

Three things stand out to me. The tiers climb fast. $10,000 of annualized premium in force, possibly fewer than a dozen policies, puts a producer at the top tier, where Prime pays agents 100% of first-year premium. Large agencies negotiate their own deals on top of that. And the rates vary far more by carrier than by product type. Ethos's own Prime term pays agents 100% at the top tier, while TruStage's term product pays 61%. Prime and Choice are products Ethos built with its carriers, so it likely earns more on them and passes more through. On Prime at the top tier, Ethos keeps only what the carrier pays above 100% of premium, plus any renewals.

What agents are selling

Ethos doesn't disclose sales by product. The S-1 said whole life is "primarily sold through our third-party channel," while direct sales have historically been more term. That was before the agent channel took off, but management has said the same thing since:

  • On the Q3 call, CFO Chris Capozzi said revenue per policy fell "as policy sales shifted more toward whole life products in the third-party channel."
  • On the Q1 call, CEO Peter Colis announced two new final expense whole life products with Banner Life, and said indexed universal life "continues to exhibit healthy growth in our third-party channel."

Final expense whole life policies are small, so as agents sell more of them, revenue per policy falls. It fell 13% year over year in Q3, to $1,655. The new Banner whole life products aren't in the pay table above, so I don't know what agents earn on them.

The disclosed split

Before the IPO, Ethos disclosed agent payments as a share of third-party revenue:

That blended share mixes every product agents sell. A Prime sale at the top tier pays the agent 100% of premium. A guaranteed acceptance whole life sale pays 30-36%. Ethos probably earns less from carriers on the low-paying products too. Without the product mix, the blended share can't be broken back into rates for individual products.

Estimating Q3 2026

Ethos's Q3 release doesn't split agent pay from advertising, but it gives enough to estimate it. Gross profit was $230.8M and contribution profit was $66.4M. The $164.3M difference is the variable cost of acquiring policies: ads, agent payouts and other per-policy costs. Direct revenue was $118.8M and third-party revenue was $116.4M. I subtract my estimate of everything besides agent pay, then divide what's left by third-party revenue.

Costs besides agent payLeft for agentsShare of third-party revenue
Ads at 36% of direct revenue, plus $21.2M other$100.4M86%
Ads at 47% of direct revenue, plus $21.2M other$87.3M75%
All direct costs at 60% of direct revenue$93.1M80%
All direct costs at 70% of direct revenue$81.2M70%

Worst case. The first two rows assume direct sales cost what the S-1 showed: advertising at 36-47% of direct revenue, plus other per-policy costs of about 9% of total revenue. That puts agents at roughly 75-86% of third-party revenue.

Conservative case. On the Q3 call, management said return on ad spend fell modestly year over year as they bought more TV, radio and social ads. So direct sales probably cost more than S-1 levels. The last two rows assume all direct costs ran 60-70% of direct revenue, which puts agents at roughly 70-80%. What's left still includes some other third-party costs, so the true agent share is likely a bit lower within the range. That's the estimate I use.

What it implies

Agents took 58-70% of third-party revenue in the S-1 years, and I estimate 70-80% in Q3. The pay table shows how that can rise without Ethos changing a single rate. The tiers top out quickly, Ethos's own term product pays agents 100% at the top, and large agencies negotiate their own deals. At the same time, agents are selling more small whole life policies, so each sale brings in less revenue. Ethos ends up with a thinner slice of smaller sales, and that's the part of the business growing fastest.

What I can't know

Ethos doesn't disclose sales by product, its carrier commission rates, what large agencies are paid, or the split between ad spend and agent pay. The 2025 10-K and the 10-Qs since the IPO don't give the agent share either. Every piece that is disclosed points the same way, though. Ethos keeps a minority of each agent sale, and that minority has likely shrunk as the agent channel went from a quarter of revenue to half.

Drew,

Sources

  • Ethos agent terms (compensation table, 12-month window, clawbacks)
  • S-1/A, January 2026 (agent payments and advertising ratios, whole life sold mainly through agents)
  • 2025 10-K
  • Q3 2026 earnings release (contribution profit, channel revenue, revenue per policy)
  • Q1 2026 earnings release ($16.5M change in estimate)
  • Q1 2026 earnings call transcript (Banner final expense products, IUL growth)
  • Q3 2026 earnings call summary (whole life mix, return on ad spend)
